    FAPD-AI: S. 933, the NASA Transition Authorization Act of 2025, as reported by the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, authorizes $25,507,540,000 in appropriations for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration for fiscal year 2025, allocated across NASA mission directorates and offices. The bill's table of contents lists titles on exploration, space operations, space technology, aeronautics, science, STEM education, and NASA policy. The sections shown in the source text include a reaffirmation of continuity of purpose for space exploration, findings and requirements for the Artemis program, and reaffirmation of the Space Launch System; the source text is truncated, and this summary covers only the sections shown.     119 S2378 RS: Spending Aviation Fees for Equipment, Guaranteeing Upgraded and Advanced Risk Detection and Safety Act of… (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119s2378rs

    FAPD-AI: S. 2378, the SAFEGUARDS Act of 2025 as reported by the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, amends 49 U.S.C. 44923 to revise the Aviation Security Capital Fund and establish an Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund. For fiscal years 2026 through 2036, it directs the TSA Administrator to collect at least $400,000,000 annually for the capital fund and at least $250,000,000 annually for the checkpoint technology fund from fees under 49 U.S.C. 44940(a)(1). The bill also requires briefings and reports to Congress, biennial Inspector General audits through fiscal year 2036, and includes a sense of Congress on the use of the 9/11 Security Fee. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 23:52:22 Eastern time ET
    119 S3226 RS: Bring Our Heroes Home Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119s3226rs

    FAPD-AI: S. 3226, the Bring Our Heroes Home Act, as reported by the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, directs the Archivist of the United States to create a Missing Armed Forces and Civilian Personnel Records Collection at the National Archives. It requires Government offices to identify, copy, and transmit to the Archivist records relating to missing Armed Forces and civilian personnel from December 7, 1941 onward, prohibits their destruction or alteration, and requires certifications under penalty of perjury. The bill also establishes a Missing Armed Forces and Civilian Personnel Records Review Board and sets requirements for reports justifying any substantial redaction or withholding of records; the source text is truncated, and this summary covers only the sections shown. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 23:52:22 Eastern time ET
    119 S4448 RS: Accelerating Broadband Permits Act of 2026 (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119s4448rs

    FAPD-AI: S. 4448, the Accelerating Broadband Permits Act of 2026, as reported by the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, directs the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information to publish a public dashboard tracking Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) grant recipients' expenditures and broadband service locations. It requires the Assistant Secretary to publish semiannual reports on BEAD grant progress, create a permit-tracking tool for eligible entities and subgrantees, develop data controls for communications use application processing times within 120 days, and establish an alert method for applications at risk of missing the 270-day deadline. The bill also amends the FAST Act definition of minimum broadband project cost to include NEPA-subject broadband infrastructure projects likely to require more than $5,000,000 in total investment. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 23:52:22 Eastern time ET
    119 S4691 RS: Disaster Communications Coordination and Preparedness Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119s4691rs

    FAPD-AI: S. 4691, the Disaster Communications Coordination and Preparedness Act, as reported without amendment by the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, directs the Federal Communications Commission to review its procedures for Disaster Information Reporting System (DIRS) activation and deactivation notices within 180 days. It requires the Commission to evaluate, within 18 months, the feasibility of enhancing its public safety liaison functions as a point of entry for State, local, Tribal, and territorial officials, and to develop plain-language awareness materials within one year. The bill states that it does not require the Commission to adopt new regulations or impose new reporting requirements on communications providers. BILLS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-25-07088 / USCOURTS-ca10-25-07088-0

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit issued an unpublished order and judgment on November 9, 2026, in Bailey v. City of Ada, No. 25-7088, arising from a police shooting in which an officer shot Jeffrey Peterson after entering his apartment without a warrant. The court affirmed the district court's grant of summary judgment to the City of Ada on plaintiff's failure-to-train claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, concluding that plaintiff did not show the city's training was inadequate. The order states that it is not binding precedent except under the doctrines of law of the case, res judicata, and collateral estoppel. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:26:29 Eastern time ET
    Travelodge Hotels Inc v. Huber Hotels LLC, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-25-02808 / USCOURTS-ca3-25-02808-0

    FAPD-AI: The Third Circuit issued a nonprecedential opinion on November 9, 2026, in Travelodge Hotels, Inc. v. Huber Hotels, LLC, No. 25-2808, on appeal from a bench-trial judgment of the District of New Jersey. The court held that the district court did not clearly err in finding that Travelodge materially breached a November 17, 2017 franchising agreement by failing to integrate a hotel in Hurley, Wisconsin into its reservation system within a reasonable time. The court affirmed the judgment in favor of Huber Hotels, LLC, Robert Huber, and Janette Huber. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:26:29 Eastern time ET
    Jennifer McDowell v. Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-01586 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-01586-0

    FAPD-AI: The Third Circuit issued a nonprecedential per curiam opinion on November 9, 2026, in McDowell v. Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, No. 26-1586, affirming the Middle District of Pennsylvania's dismissal with prejudice of pro se plaintiff Jennifer E. McDowell's amended complaint. The court found that the complaint's allegations of a statewide conspiracy by the Department of Human Services' Child Welfare Department were conclusory and did not state a plausible claim under Ashcroft v. Iqbal, and that further amendment would be futile. The court also denied McDowell's request to supplement the appellate record with extra-record allegations. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:26:29 Eastern time ET
    John Gomez v. City of Pittsburgh, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-01735 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-01735-0

    FAPD-AI: The Third Circuit issued a nonprecedential per curiam opinion on November 9, 2026, in Gomez v. City of Pittsburgh, No. 26-1735, affirming the Western District of Pennsylvania's Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal of John Paul Gomez's amended complaint under 42 U.S.C. § 1983. The court held that Gomez identified no source for a duty to notify him of his ex-wife's 2019 arrest, and that his claims regarding the search and arrest of his adult son either could not be asserted by him or rested on conclusory allegations. The court did not reach the district court's alternative statute-of-limitations ruling. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Miracle, et al v. Hush, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-25-03032 / USCOURTS-ca10-25-03032-0

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit issued a published opinion on November 9, 2026, in Miracle v. Hush, No. 25-3032, on an interlocutory appeal concerning whether qualified immunity extends to Emporia State University personnel and Kansas Board of Regents members regarding the termination of nine tenured professors. The court addressed the case at the motion-to-dismiss stage, based on the allegations of the complaint, and stated that it affirms in part and reverses in part. The opinion recites that plaintiffs allege they were terminated under a temporary 2021 amendment to the Board of Regents' Workforce Management Plan because of their political beliefs and activities.     FAPD-AI: A memorandum dated November 10, 2026, from the President to the Secretaries of the Interior and Agriculture and the EPA Administrator determines that firefighting activities, including aerial use of fire retardants by the Forest Service, the Department of the Interior, other agencies, and their contractors, are exempt from Federal, State, interstate, and local water pollution control requirements under section 313 of the Federal Water Pollution Control Act, except for requirements under 33 U.S.C. 1316 and 1317.     Montanez Berrios v. Samaniego (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-50320 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-50320-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 9, 2026, the Fifth Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of Deliris Montanez Berrios's second Rule 60(b) motion to reopen her suit against El Paso County Judge Ricardo Samaniego and Texas Secretary of State Robert S. Howden, and denied her motion for an injunction pending appeal. The court held that the motions to reopen were filed after the 28-day Rule 59 period and therefore did not toll the time to appeal, and that the appellate briefing did not identify a Rule 60(b) ground for relief. The panel also held that the injunction factors were not established, because the election records at issue were not shown to be at risk of loss. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:33:40 Eastern time ET
    Ibrahim v. Blanche (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-60122 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-60122-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 9, 2026, the Fifth Circuit denied the petition for review filed by Joul Ghasan Ibrahim, a native and citizen of Syria, of a Board of Immigration Appeals decision affirming the denial of asylum, withholding of removal, and relief under the Convention Against Torture. The court held that the petitioner forfeited challenges to the BIA's determination that the petitioner had waived challenges under the Circumvention of Lawful Pathways rule, and that the petitioner did not show that no reasonable factfinder could make the adverse credibility determination. The court also found that the BIA had considered the country conditions evidence, and that general country conditions evidence did not establish an individualized risk of torture. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: On November 9, 2026, the Fifth Circuit issued an unpublished per curiam opinion in Carroll v. Turner Industries Group, No. 26-30230, affirming the Western District of Louisiana's denial of a motion to vacate an arbitration award. The arbitrator, applying the parties' Dispute Resolution Agreement and the AAA Employment Rules, dismissed the plaintiff's Americans with Disabilities Act and Texas law claims as unexhausted with the EEOC or TWC and time-barred.     FAPD-AI: On November 9, 2026, the Fifth Circuit issued an unpublished per curiam opinion in Alcala v. Unity One Credit Union, No. 26-40030, affirming the Eastern District of Texas's dismissal of the plaintiff's claims against Unity One Credit Union. A magistrate judge, acting by consent, granted Rule 12(b)(6) motions by Unity and Bosco Auto Group and dismissed the claims with prejudice. The court held that the plaintiff did not plead sufficient facts to state claims under the Truth in Lending Act, the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act, or Texas repossession law, and that the consolidation and with-prejudice dismissal were not abuses of discretion. The court noted that Weber did not challenge the failure-to-prosecute determination on review.     FAPD-AI: The Federal Circuit issued a nonprecedential per curiam decision in Bruzzese v. MSPB, No. 2026-1704, affirming the Board's dismissal of Adam Bruzzese's Individual Right of Action whistleblower appeal on collateral estoppel grounds. The court found that his 2024 claims, which challenged a 2009 reassignment at the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms as retaliatory and as a denial of due process, were identical to claims raised and decided in a 2020 Board appeal. It further found that the 2020 issues were actually litigated, were necessary to that decision, and that Bruzzese had represented himself in that proceeding. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: Rep. Massie gave notice of his intent to raise a question of the privileges of the House by offering a resolution to impeach Peter Brian Hegseth, Secretary of Defense. The draft articles of impeachment allege that Hegseth directed U.S. Armed Forces into hostilities against Iran beginning February 28, 2026, without a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization, or a national emergency as described in the War Powers Resolution of 1973. The articles further allege that hostilities continued after H. Con. Res. 86, a concurrent resolution directing removal of the forces, was agreed to by the House on June 3, 2026, and by the Senate on June 23, 2026. CREC-SEL-01

    Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act (opens in a new tab)
    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2026-11-09 / CREC-2026-11-09-pt1-PgH6097

    FAPD-AI: The House considered H.R. 5549, the Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act, under suspension of the rules. The bill amends the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 to remove the requirement that the Nuclear Regulatory Commission hold a hearing on a construction permit or operating license application when no person requests one, allowing issuance after 30 days' notice and Federal Register publication, while preserving hearings requested by affected persons and applying the amendments to pending proceedings. The floor debate includes statements from Representatives Latta, Pallone, and Griffith on the bill's provisions and on the estimated cost of uncontested hearings to applicants. CREC-SEL-01

    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2026-11-09 / CREC-2026-11-09-pt1-PgH6100

    FAPD-AI: The House considered H.R. 9612, the American Enrichment Deployment Act, under suspension of the rules, as amended. The bill amends section 193 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 to permit construction of uranium enrichment facilities before a license is issued, under the same terms that apply to other fuel cycle facilities, and directs the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to issue or revise implementing regulations within 180 days of enactment. The text states that the National Environmental Policy Act, the right to a hearing under section 189, and NRC inspection authority are not affected, and the debate includes statements from Representatives Latta, Pallone, and Fry.     Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES · FR-2026-11-10 / 2026-22865

    official summary: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or we) is partially granting a color additive petition submitted by Environmental Defense Fund et al. (petitioners), by amending our color additive regulations, on the basis of the Delaney Clause, to remove the authorized use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables. The petitioners provided data demonstrating that this additive induces cancer in laboratory animals. We are denying the remaining petition requests to remove ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene from the list of authorized extraction solvents for annatto extract, paprika oleoresin, and turmeric oleoresin, because any residue of the solvent would be an impurity in the color additive and such impurities are not subject to the Delaney Clause. FR-SEL-01

    official summary: The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain Airbus SAS Model A350-941 airplanes. This AD was prompted by a report of a missing main landing gear (MLG) brake rod center pin nut sub-assembly detected during an inspection. This AD requires, depending on airplane configuration, inspection of the MLG brake rod center pin nut, lock ring, and end plate, inspection of the MLG brake rod center pin and nut, and applicable corrective actions. This AD also requires additional work for certain airplanes. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. FR-SEL-01

    Unemployment Insurance Program National Minimum Weekly Work Search Requirements (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF LABOR · FR-2026-11-10 / 2026-22903

    official summary: The U.S. Department of Labor (Department), through the Employment and Training Administration (ETA), is proposing to amend 20 CFR part 604 both to reflect a 2012 update in Federal law in which Congress, by amending section 303(a) of the Social Security Act (SSA), established a Federal work search requirement; and to establish a national minimum weekly work search requirement standard for the Federal-State unemployment compensation (UC) program. This proposed rule would mandate, among other things, that States require individuals claiming UC to complete at least five qualifying work search activities or, where applicable, meet State-adopted points-based system requirements amounting to five qualifying activities or satisfy equivalent labor force attachment criteria, each week for which UC is claimed; that individuals report their work search activities as part of their certification process prior to payment being issued; and that State law allow for certain qualifying work search activities beyond simply employer contacts. This action is necessary to reduce inconsistencies beyond those created by local labor markets in State-level requirements for individuals to actively seek work. [official summary truncated; see source] FR-SEL-02

    Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program: Reforming Categorical Eligibility (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE · FR-2026-11-10 / 2026-22936

    official summary: Under section 5(a) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, households in which each member receives benefits under a State program funded by Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) are categorically eligible for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Current SNAP regulations consider TANF benefits to include both cash assistance and non-cash or in-kind benefits or services from TANF-funded programs. This proposal would limit categorical eligibility to only households that receive TANF assistance, as defined at 45 CFR 260.31. These revisions would ensure that SNAP benefits are targeted to needy households that have qualified for TANF assistance while still aligning categorical eligibility's statutory purpose of simplifying program administration. A 100-word summary of this rule has been posted to www.regulations.gov and can be found here. FR-SEL-02

    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE · FR-2026-11-10 / 2026-22944

    official summary: The proposed rule would codify USDA's regulatory implementation of provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 (OBBB) changing the three-month time limit for certain participants subject to work requirements in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). These changes include modifying the list of exceptions from the time limit for certain populations; updating requirements for areas to qualify for waivers of the time limit; and adding the temporary good faith exemptions in Alaska and Hawaii. Additionally, this rule proposes to strengthen requirements for requesting waivers of the time limit and revise the SNAP definition of a homeless individual. FR-SEL-02

    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION · FR-2026-11-10 / 2026-22951

    official summary: These special conditions are issued for the Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation (Gulfstream) Model GVII-G400 airplane. This airplane will have a novel or unusual design feature when compared to the state of technology envisioned in the airworthiness standards for transport category airplanes. This design feature is an envelope protection function to protect the airplane from over- and rapid-rotation on takeoff. The applicable airworthiness regulations do not contain adequate or appropriate safety standards for this design feature. These special conditions contain the additional safety standards that the Administrator considers necessary to establish a level of safety equivalent to that established by the existing airworthiness standards. FR-SEL-01

    official summary: The final rule updates the maintenance inspection requirements for single-engine turbine-powered airplanes and unmanned aircraft. Aircraft owners and operators now have more inspection program options to choose from and more relaxed mechanical reliability reporting requirements. It also clarifies various maintenance-related regulations. This final rule relieves aircraft owners, operators, maintenance providers, and FAA of certain workload burdens by facilitating a more efficient workload for these individuals without compromising aviation safety.
